title: Song of Solomon 1:8–17
context: The dialogue continues. The WEB assigns verses 8–10 to the Lover, who answers the Beloved’s question with pastoral directions and praises her with images drawn from royal horses and jewelry; verse 11 to the Friends, who promise ornaments of gold and silver; verses 12–14 and 16 to the Beloved; and verses 15 and 17 to the Lover. Attributions in this kind of rapid exchange vary among interpreters. The images come from the world of the poem: the king at his table, fragrant perfume and spices, henna blossoms from the vineyards of En Gedi (compare 1 Samuel 23:29), doves, and a shelter of cedar and fir. Readers who take the Song literally commonly see mutual admiration, delight, and a shared home as marks of covenant love. Readers who take it figuratively commonly hear the mutual delight between God and his people, or between Christ and the church. Arminian and Reformed readers both include holders of each view, and both commonly treat the passage as shared ground about the goodness of faithful love.

verses.text: If you don’t know, most beautiful among women, follow the tracks of the sheep. Graze your young goats beside the shepherds’ tents.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Lover, as the WEB labels him, answering gently with directions to follow the tracks of the sheep. Love responds to honest seeking.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the reply as tender guidance. Figurative readers commonly hear a call to follow the paths of the flock and the shepherds, an image of finding Christ among his people.

verses.text: I have compared you, my love, to a steed in Pharaoh’s chariots.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Lover praising the Beloved with an image from royal chariots, a compliment of beauty and dignity in its ancient setting.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the comparison as honor drawn from the splendor of Pharaoh’s horses. Readers in both traditions commonly read it as admiration rather than pressing every detail.

verses.text: Your cheeks are beautiful with earrings, your neck with strings of jewels.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Lover delighting in the Beloved adorned with earrings and jewels. Adornment expresses honor and celebration.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see admiration that delights in the beloved’s beauty. Figurative readers commonly hear the beauty God gives to his people, as both traditions often note.

verses.text: We will make you earrings of gold, with studs of silver.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Friends promising earrings of gold with studs of silver. The community adds its gifts to the celebration of love.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see generous gifts from those who rejoice with the couple. Figurative readers commonly hear the adornment of the church with gifts that enhance her beauty.

verses.text: While the king sat at his table, my perfume spread its fragrance.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Beloved describing her perfume spreading its fragrance while the king sat at his table. Love is pictured as a pleasing presence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an image of devotion offered in the king’s presence. Figurative readers commonly hear the worship of God’s people rising like fragrance before their King.

verses.text: My beloved is to me a sachet of myrrh, that lies between my breasts.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Beloved describing her beloved as a sachet of myrrh, an image of treasured, close affection. Literal readers see faithful nearness in marriage.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an image of the beloved kept close to the heart. Figurative readers commonly hear the believer cherishing Christ, and both traditions read the line with restraint.

verses.text: My beloved is to me a cluster of henna blossoms from the vineyards of En Gedi.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Beloved comparing him to henna blossoms from the vineyards of En Gedi. Delight is expressed through the beauty of a well-known oasis.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image as a picture of fragrance and freshness. Readers in both traditions commonly appreciate the poetry without forcing a detailed allegorical meaning.

verses.text: Behold, you are beautiful, my love. Behold, you are beautiful. Your eyes are like doves.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Lover twice declaring the Beloved beautiful and praising her eyes as doves. Love speaks words of affirmation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see admiration expressed in gentle images. Figurative readers commonly hear the love with which Christ regards his church, an image shared across both traditions.

verses.text: Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, yes, pleasant; and our couch is verdant.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Beloved answering with her own praise of him and speaking of their shared couch as verdant. Love is mutual and joyful.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see reciprocal delight and a flourishing life together. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as celebrating the mutual joy of covenant love.

verses.text: The beams of our house are cedars. Our rafters are firs.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Lover describing their house with beams of cedar and rafters of fir. Love builds a shared and lasting dwelling.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image of a secure home. Figurative readers commonly hear the dwelling God makes with his people, with both traditions holding literal and figurative readings.
